title: The Manual
author: Epictetus (recorded by Arrian)
openingText: Some things are in our control and others not. Things in our control are opinion, pursuit, desire, aversion, and, in a word, whatever are our own actions. Things not in our control are body, reputation, command, and, in one word, whatever are not our own actions.
about:
The Manual — Encheiridion in Greek, literally something held in the hand — is a short Stoic guide compiled around 125 CE by Arrian from the lectures of his teacher Epictetus. Its first sentence states the whole system. Some things are in our control; others are not. The chapters that follow apply that distinction to anger, grief, ambition, fear, social embarrassment, the death of family members, the loss of property, and the management of one's own thoughts. Each chapter is short, designed to be read and reread until the principle has become reflexive.

Epictetus had been born a slave in Phrygia around 55 CE. He was lame, possibly from a beating; he was taken to Rome, where his master allowed him to study Stoic philosophy under Musonius Rufus; he was eventually freed and set up his own school. When the emperor Domitian banished philosophers from Rome around 89 CE, Epictetus moved to Nicopolis on the western coast of Greece and taught there for the rest of his life. Arrian, his student — later a Roman governor and the historian of Alexander's campaigns — took down his lectures in eight books, four of which survive as the Discourses. The Manual is Arrian's distillation of the most essential passages.

The book is the most concentrated expression of Stoic ethics ever written. Focus on what is in your power; accept what is not; judge events by your responses to them rather than by the events themselves. The aphoristic format is deliberate. Epictetus is not building a system for theorists. He is giving someone a tool to carry into the next argument with a spouse, the next bad news from a doctor, the next humiliation in public. Marcus Aurelius's Meditations are unimaginable without him.

angleCards.title: The dichotomy of control.
angleCards.text: Epictetus's whole system rests on a single distinction: what is up to us and what is not. I want to work through each chapter testing whether that distinction is real — whether it actually holds under pressure, or whether it is a consoling simplification.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to test the dichotomy of control — what is actually within my power and what is not — and whether it holds up as a true description of human experience.

angleCards.title: A slave writing about freedom.
angleCards.text: Epictetus was owned. He lost his external freedom completely, and that is precisely the context in which he developed a philosophy of inner freedom. I want to read the text with that biography in mind and see whether it adds weight or complicates his claims.
angleCards.angleObjective: I'm reading Epictetus as a former slave writing about freedom — and I want to understand what that context does to his philosophy, whether it makes it more or less credible.

angleCards.title: Reading it as practice.
angleCards.text: Epictetus didn't write for theorists — he wrote for people who wanted to change how they live. The Enchiridion is meant to be worked, not just read. I want to treat each chapter as an exercise and notice what actually shifts when I try to apply it.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the Enchiridion as a practice, not a text — working through the exercises as Epictetus intended, not just understanding the arguments intellectually.

angleCards.title: The Stoic theory of emotion.
angleCards.text: Stoics didn't say don't feel — they said don't be ruled by feelings that rest on false judgments. I want to follow their emotional theory carefully, understand what they actually claimed, and decide whether modern psychology has proved them right or wrong.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to understand the Stoic theory of emotion — why they thought passion clouded judgment, whether they were right, and what the alternative looks like in practice.

cast.name: Epictetus
cast.description: Born a slave in Hierapolis around 55 CE, lame from a beating or a congenital condition, he became a freedman, a philosopher, and the founder of a school at Nicopolis. He taught for free to anyone who came. He never wrote anything down. His lectures, taken down by his student Arrian, are the basis of both the Discourses and the Manual. The voice in the text is direct, unsentimental, and habitually addressed to a particular student in the room being told to stop making the same mistake.

cast.name: Arrian
cast.description: A young Greek of equestrian rank from Nicomedia who studied with Epictetus around 108 CE, took down his lectures verbatim, and later compiled the Manual from the most essential passages. Arrian went on to a successful Roman career — consul, governor of Cappadocia, military commander — and wrote the standard history of Alexander's campaigns. Without him, the philosophy of the most influential late Stoic teacher would have been lost entirely.

cast.name: The Dichotomy of Control
cast.description: The division between what is in our power — opinion, desire, aversion, the use of impressions, our own actions — and what is not — the body, property, reputation, the actions of others, the events of the world. Every other teaching in the manual follows from getting this distinction right. Almost all human suffering, Epictetus argues, comes from confusing one with the other: investing identity in things that can be taken away, neglecting the only things that cannot.

cast.name: The Hegemonikon
cast.description: The Stoic term for the governing part of the soul — the faculty of judgment, of assent, of choosing how to interpret an impression. What Epictetus means when he says you. Not your body, not your possessions, not your reputation, but the thing inside that decides whether the slave who broke the cup is a catastrophe or a small fact. The whole practice of the Manual is the training and protection of this faculty against the impressions that constantly try to override it.

cast.name: Marcus Aurelius
cast.description: Roman emperor from 161 to 180 CE and Stoic practitioner whose Meditations are essentially private notes applying Epictetus's teaching to the daily life of an emperor. He cites Epictetus by name and quotes him repeatedly. He is the most famous reader of this text and the proof Epictetus most often offered without knowing he was offering it: that the philosophy can be lived in extreme conditions, including the conditions of supreme worldly power.

cast.name: Zeno of Citium
cast.description: A Phoenician-Greek merchant who was shipwrecked at Athens around 300 BCE, took up philosophy, and founded the Stoic school in the painted colonnade — the Stoa Poikile — that gave the movement its name. He taught that virtue is the only good and that everything else is indifferent. Epictetus is his heir three centuries later, adapting and sharpening the tradition and giving it the personal urgency of someone who had, before he was free, tested the philosophy under conditions Zeno never faced.

whyItMatters.title: A Practical Stoicism
whyItMatters.body: Where most ancient philosophy is theoretical, the Manual is operational. It tells you what to do when you are angry. It tells you what to do when someone insults you. It tells you what to do when your child dies, or when you have lost something you cannot replace. The instructions are concrete: when you kiss your child goodnight, remind yourself that the child is mortal and may not be alive in the morning, so that if death comes it will not destroy you. The aphoristic format is designed for daily reference, not for systematic reading. Epictetus assumes you will reread the same chapter many times, in different states, and that the words will land differently each time.

whyItMatters.title: What Is in Your Control
whyItMatters.body: The book opens with the most important distinction in Stoic philosophy. Some things are in our control; others are not. Mistaking one for the other, Epictetus argues, is the source of most suffering. You cannot control the rain, the traffic, your colleague's bad opinion of you, your body's slow decline, your child's choices, or whether the people you love will outlive you. You can control your judgment about each of these things, the meaning you assign to them, and the action you choose in response. The category is small. It is also entirely sufficient for the parts of life that matter most. The principle has shaped not just Stoicism but most of the cognitive behavioral therapy now practiced — Aaron Beck and Albert Ellis both cited Epictetus as a direct influence on the techniques they were formalizing in the 1950s and 60s.

whyItMatters.title: A Slave's Philosophy
whyItMatters.body: Epictetus had been a slave. He knew, more concretely than any Stoic before him, what the loss of external control feels like — what it is to have your body, your time, your geography, your name, all decided by someone else. The Manual is the most extreme test case for Stoic philosophy. Does the practice work when external freedom is genuinely absent, when there is no possibility of fixing the situation through political action or wealth or status? Epictetus's answer is the entire book. Whether his answer is sufficient is one of the longest-running arguments in the philosophy of freedom; the question continues to be raised in prison memoirs, hospice writing, and accounts of life under tyranny.
